Assessing Generalization in AI-Generated Music Detection

Angelos-Nikolaos Kanatas1, David López-Ayala1, Pablo Zinemanas2, Martín Rocamora1, Xavier Serra1, Dmitry Bogdanov1

1Music Technology Group, Universitat Pompeu Fabra, Barcelona
2BMAT Licensing, Barcelona

Paper Data Code
AbstractKey resultsExploreListenGlossaryFamily exclusionsGenerators, all families presentArtifactNetWithheld generatorsDecoder classesCross-corpus pairsStrictly unseenGenerators per pairMUSIC8KHuman poolsThresholdsInventoryRobustnessReproducibility and dataOutside the test sets

Abstract

AI-generated music detectors perform well on data resembling their training distribution, but evaluations on new corpora change generators and human-made music at once, so failures of generalization are hard to attribute. We evaluate spectral-artifact detectors, frozen-encoder readouts and retrained baselines under three conditions: generator families absent from training, changes in the human-made music a detector is compared against, and whether a threshold calibrated on one corpus holds on another. A family exclusion withholds all versions of one provider from a multi-corpus training pool and is compared with a size-matched pool that retains them. Spectral-template detectors incur larger mean AUROC losses than frozen-encoder readouts. With generated recordings fixed, AUROC varies more across human-made sets for the evaluated representation-based methods than for spectral detectors. A learned combination of encoder and spectral scores achieves .928 mean AUROC over nine cross-corpus evaluations, exceeding its components and retrained baselines. A threshold calibrated on the training corpus can produce excessive false alarms on another corpus; for a 5% target, recalibrating the learned combination on 200 human-made recordings of the test corpus yields 4.3% false alarms and 76.1% detection. Generalization to unseen generator families, sensitivity to human-made sets and threshold reuse across corpora require separate evaluation.

This page disaggregates the paper's two tables: each family exclusion, each generator, each training–test pair, each human-made pool, and both decision thresholds. Every value is recomputed from the saved per-recording scores of the fitted detectors; nothing was refitted for this page, and the rows printed in the paper are reproduced before any table is written (S14, Reproducibility). AUROC throughout, higher is better; a loss is AUROC with a family withheld minus AUROC under the size-matched control. AB is ArtifactBench, FMC is FakeMusicCaps, M8K is MUSIC8K; detector names follow the paper's tables. Three parts go beyond the paper's tables and are marked so: Table S11c, S13 and S15 score the same fitted detectors, with nothing refit, on inputs the paper does not evaluate. Figures and tables are numbered S1–S15 so that the paper can cite them.

How to read this page. The menu below jumps to each table. Column headers sort; hovering a cell shows the values behind it; the selectors above a table choose the test corpus, the comparison or the metric; every table can be downloaded as CSV beside its controls, and the complete unrounded bundle is linked in S14.

Key results

The headline number, then the paper's three conditions in one number each (both detector families, with the control or the fixed side named), then five views that the paper's tables compress into single numbers. Colors follow the paper's figure: fusion, spectral templates, fingerprint, trajectory readout, mean and attention pooling, retrained baselines.

Reading the tables against the paper. (1) Withholding a family costs the spectral templates .16–.18 of mean AUROC and the representation readouts .03–.08 (Table S1), yet on the withheld families the templates remain the more accurate member under the control (.96 against .92) and the less accurate after exclusion (.78 against .84); what transfers is the decoder, not the brand: unseen RVQ generators score .95–1.00 under the templates, every Udio subset .33–.48 (Table S7). (2) With the generated recordings fixed, the AUROC range across human-made pools is .05–.08 for the spectral detectors, .12–.14 for the MuQ readouts and .15–.28 for the retrained baselines (Table S10). (3) A threshold set at 5% false alarms on the training corpus produces 14–38% on FakeMusicCaps for the MuQ readouts although that corpus is a middle pool by AUROC: the shift is in score scale, not ranking; recalibrating on 200 human-made recordings restores the rate at a cost in detection (Table S11). S15 tests the same fitted detectors on recordings the paper does not evaluate.

Notes on the protocol

Family exclusions (Table 1 of the paper). Training combines the other two test corpora with SONICS. A family is withheld from training and validation wherever it occurs; the size-matched control keeps it but subsamples generated recordings to the exclusion count within each corpus and split. Both models score the same test recordings of that family against the same human-made recordings of the test corpus. The six primary comparisons (Suno and Udio in ArtifactBench and Echoes; MusicGen in ArtifactBench and FakeMusicCaps) were selected first; the seven comparisons with Stable Audio, AudioLDM and DiffRhythm were added afterwards. Every comparison rests on one fitted model per arm and one control draw; the intervals shown resample recordings with the fitted models fixed.

Cross-corpus transfer (Table 2 of the paper). One training corpus, one test corpus. Nine pairs enter the summary; SONICS test corpora are excluded because bandwidth alone separates the classes there. MUSIC8K averages the four single-corpus models against the same 1,102 FakeMusicCaps human-made recordings.

Per-generator values. A generator's AUROC is computed from its recordings against all human-made recordings of the same test corpus. Subsets under 40 recordings are marked with a dagger and are descriptive. Decoder classes are annotations from public specifications; proprietary services are marked undisclosed, and no per-recording mechanism is attributed.

Not included. MusicDET and CoMoE were not run on the seven additional comparisons (MusicDET fits human-made recordings only, so withholding a generated family cannot change it). Per-generator results for the released ArtifactNet exist only where per-recording scores exist (ArtifactBench, Echoes, MUSIC8K). No acoustic duplicate audit was performed across corpora; leakage control is by recorded identity, prompt and reference groups.

Glossary

Family exclusion
All versions of one provider (Suno, Udio, MusicGen, and so on) withheld from the multi-corpus training and validation data wherever they occur.
Size-matched control
The same training pool with the family kept, but with generated recordings subsampled per corpus and split to the count left after exclusion; human-made recordings unchanged.
Exclusion loss
AUROC of the exclusion model minus AUROC of its control on identical recordings of the withheld family; negative values mean poorer detection after exclusion.
Cross-corpus pair
A detector trained on one corpus and tested on another, so generated and human-made recordings change together; nine pairs enter the paper's summary.
Strictly unseen
Generated recordings of a test corpus whose brand and annotated decoder class are both absent from the training corpus; Table S7c lists what each corpus contains.
Decoder class
The kind of waveform decoder a generator uses, annotated from public specifications: RVQ codec (EnCodec, X-Codec), continuous VAE, mel VAE with a HiFi-GAN vocoder, spectrogram inversion, or undisclosed for proprietary services.
Human-made pool
One set of human-made recordings, grouped by corpus and origin, paired with the fixed MUSIC8K generated scores; the range is highest minus lowest AUROC over the pools outside the training corpus.
Carried and recalibrated thresholds
Carried: the training corpus's 5 percent false-alarm threshold applied unchanged. Recalibrated: the same order-statistic rule on 200 human-made recordings of the test corpus, which are then excluded from evaluation.

S11. Decision thresholds, carried and recalibrated

Table S11a. Six training-test pairs with at least 200 held-out human-made recordings of the test corpus (Echoes excluded). Carried: the training corpus's 5% threshold applied unchanged. Recalibrated: the same rule on 200 human-made recordings of the test corpus, which are then excluded from evaluation; both thresholds are evaluated on identical recordings within a system. Means are balanced over training corpora as in the paper's figure.

Table S11b. What n held-out recordings buy. The rule flags a recording when its score exceeds the ceil((n+1)(1−α))-th smallest of n held-out human-made scores. When calibration and evaluation recordings share a distribution, the realised false-alarm rate of one calibration draw follows a Beta(n+1−r, r) law (r the rank used), so n sets how far the realised rate can sit from the target. Computed here, not scored.

Table S11c. What recalibration costs at home (beyond the paper, from the same scores). A detector recalibrated on 200 human-made recordings of another corpus carries that new threshold back to the corpus it was trained on. For each detector, averaged over the six pairs of Table S11a: the false-alarm and detection rates on the training corpus's own held-out test recordings under its original 5% threshold, and under the threshold recalibrated on the other corpus. The target-side rates reproduce Table S11a exactly before this table is written. Adaptation studies report this 'forgetting' column beside the adapted rate; here no model is retrained, only the threshold moves.

The balanced over training corpora means are those of the paper's Figure 1. The Beta law is the conditional-coverage result for split conformal prediction (Angelopoulos and Bates, 2023), applied to the one-sided rank rule; when ceil((n+1)(1−α)) exceeds n the rule is undefined and no threshold exists.

S13. Robustness to processing

Beyond the paper. The paper reports no robustness result; this section scores the paper's fitted detectors (nothing refit) on processed versions of one test corpus, under the paper's own threshold rule.

Table S13. The FakeMusicCaps test split under one processing operation applied to both classes (a speed change by a factor drawn per recording from 0.7 to 1.4, a pitch shift of up to ±2 semitones, a time stretch by 0.8 to 1.2, white noise at 20 dB SNR, one peaking EQ filter (200–4000 Hz, ±6 dB), reverb with T60 0.3–0.8 s, a low-pass filter at 3.5–6 kHz, and MP3, AAC and Opus round trips at 64 kbps; every parameter is drawn per recording from a seed of its name, so a recording receives the same processing for every detector), scored by detectors trained on one corpus. One rule throughout: the 5% rank rule on 200 clean FakeMusicCaps recordings (20 draws), frozen before the operation and applied to the processed recordings; AUROC on the processed set. The clean column is the same threshold on the unprocessed set and equals the paper's Table 2 cell for that detector and training corpus (checked when this page is built, tolerance .002; detectors whose saved harvest does not reproduce the printed number on all three training corpora are left out and listed below). The published checkpoints' loaders drop length-changed clips under speed and stretch, so their cells there have fewer recordings (hover shows n). This block was part of the submitted draft and was removed for length.

Reading. The two operations that change the sample-rate ratio of the content (speed, and the pitch shift, whose phase-vocoder stretch is followed by a resampling) are the costly ones for every detector, and the cost does not grow with the amount: the three-support template loses .22–.29 AUROC under either (ArtifactBench .945 to .725 and .698; Echoes .982 to .738 and .709; SONICS .920 to .667 and .632) and at most .006 under the three codecs, the fingerprint falls to chance, while the phase-vocoder stretch alone costs little. A check outside the saved sets (not shown) found a 0.1% change of the sample rate sufficient and an integer-ratio resampling and back harmless: the templates read the decoder's exact frequency grid, and any scaling of it moves the evidence. The codecs cost the readouts more than the templates (MP3 64 kbps: attention pooling −.065 / −.025 / −.146 for the three training corpora, SpecTTTra −.132 / −.047 / −.220). The learned fusion keeps .80 or more under every operation when trained on ArtifactBench or Echoes (floors .811 and .802, both under pitch) and falls to .63–.67 under pitch and speed when trained on SONICS.

The operating point. Switch the value selector to false alarms: the MP3 round trip that leaves the fixed fusion's AUROC intact raises its false alarms at the frozen threshold to .14 / .08 / .28, and its fingerprint member's to .31 / .21 / .91; the trajectory readout's to .11 / .05 / .23. The two templates stay within .064 under every operation except reverb on the SONICS-trained models (.078 and .101) and lose detection instead (three-support under speed: .76 to .21, .92 to .23, .67 to .15). The two failure directions are therefore different: codecs shift the readout and fingerprint scores (a threshold failure, ranking intact), warps move the comb out of the templates' lag range (a ranking failure, false alarms intact).

Sources: output/analysis/learned_fusion_attack/metrics.csv (learned fusion, attention pooling, three-support; publication checkpoints, scored 2026-09-29), fixed_fusion_attack/metrics.csv (fixed fusion, single-support, fingerprint; scored 2026-10-01 at the publication members, scripts/fixed_fusion_under_attack.py), attack_metrics_<trainer>.json (trajectory readout) and baseline_attack_rates.json (SpecTTTra, CLAM, MusicDET), the last two recorded before submission.

S15. The published detectors outside the paper's test sets

Beyond the paper. The paper's fitted detectors (the same checkpoints as Table 2, nothing refitted; the fingerprint is the paper's deterministic recipe) scored on recordings the paper does not evaluate: the test recordings of each corpus after one delivery chain, a large external human-made collection, and mixtures of generated and human-made recordings. All three tables use the paper's own thresholds. Only rows whose unprocessed scores reproduce the paper's Table 2 cell within .002 are shown; the one pair that cannot be reproduced row for row is listed below the table.

Table S15a. Delivery. Every test recording of a corpus (both classes) was loudness-normalised to −23 LUFS and passed through an MP3 128 kbps round trip, the chain of a streaming upload; the originals and these twins are scored by the detector trained on another corpus. The threshold is the trainer's own 5% rule on its held-out humans, carried unchanged (the paper's Condition 3), and, as a second reading, a 5% rule set on 200 of the target's unprocessed humans (20 draws). The question is whether a detector that passes the paper's cross-corpus test keeps its false-alarm rate when the same humans arrive through a common delivery chain.

Reading.

Table S15b. Genre. 24,696 human-made FMA-medium tracks (30 s, one delivery chain, eleven genres with 380 or more tracks), scored by each published detector at its trainer's own 5% threshold; the table shows the false-alarm rate per genre and overall. The fingerprint and the single-support template have no trainer-side threshold in the paper and carry a 200-human rule set on clean FakeMusicCaps humans instead. The last two columns are the 1% and 0.1% points set on half of the FMA tracks and read on the other half: how well a rule transfers within one delivery chain, not across corpora.

Reading.

Table S15c. Partial generation. Each generated FakeMusicCaps test clip mixed with its caption-paired human-made recording, x = (1 − a) h + a g at equal RMS and one level per pair, so a is the generated fraction by amplitude; scored by the same published detectors at the clean 5% rule (200 clean FakeMusicCaps humans, 20 draws; false alarms on the unmixed humans stay at 4–6% for every detector). The a = 1 column is the clean row of Table S13. An incoherent sum of two unrelated recordings, not an edit or a continuation.
